title: The hypertrophy series: muscular vs cardiovascular fatigue
summary: He distinguishes muscular fatigue (fiber micro-damage that reduces force output and drives hypertrophy through recovery) from cardiovascular fatigue (being out of breath), which many 'fatigue-seeking' YouTube programs mistake for an effective stimulus. The goal is enough damage without injury, around maximum recoverable volume, with enough recovery time; soreness is a poor recovery indicator.

claims.claim: Hypertrophy works by damaging muscle fibers in training, then rebuilding them bigger and stronger through food and rest; this is what he calls muscular fatigue.
Muscular fatigue reduces a fiber's ability to produce force, after which it recovers bigger and stronger.
Muscular and cardiovascular fatigue sometimes go together but must not be confused; many 'fatigue-seeking' methods actually target cardiovascular fatigue.
A lot of YouTube fitness has people training to exhaustion, but being exhausted doesn't mean you'll grow; an exercise that leaves you out of breath isn't necessarily a good hypertrophy exercise.
Squatting 20% of your back squat non-stop causes burning from lactic acid and ragged breathing, but that's cardiovascular fatigue, not an effective muscular stimulus.
Too much damage becomes injury (a tear within the muscle or detachment from the tendon); the aim is enough damage to recover from without injury, plus enough time before training it again.
The target amount of muscular damage is your maximum recoverable volume, which keeps changing, so you must keep adapting.
Deliberately stopping short of full muscular fatigue on one day and finishing the muscle a day or two later is a valid tactic.
You can judge recovery by the common 48-hour rule or by feel, but checking whether a muscle is sore to the touch is inaccurate, since soreness can last a week.
